problem: Prior deep-learning navigation agents cannot navigate to image-specified goals in previously unseen 3D environments using only a short visual walkthrough. They fall into three groups. Reactive agents have no memory. LSTM agents cannot store roughly 10k-step walkthrough footage. Metric-map agents (Neural Map, CMP, SLAM-augmented DRL) need ground-truth ego-motion, poses or depth. RL agents such as Mirowski et al. were also trained and tested in the same environment rather than on new layouts.
motivation: Psychology evidence suggests animals and humans rely on landmark and topological knowledge rather than metric cognitive maps. Metric SLAM is also brittle: it is sensitive to calibration, poor imaging and dynamic scenes. The observation driving the paper is that a non-metric graph of stored observations, with a learned similarity function for localization and loop closure plus a learned short-range controller, can support long-horizon planning with no pose or ego-motion information and no reward signal.
key_idea: Build a topological graph whose nodes are raw observations from an exploration walkthrough. Edges come from temporal adjacency plus learned visual-similarity shortcuts. A self-supervised siamese retrieval network localizes the agent and the goal in the graph, Dijkstra finds a path, and a self-supervised locomotion network drives the agent to the furthest confidently reachable waypoint on that path.
insight: Two things make long-range navigation from a short walkthrough possible. First, temporal-proximity self-supervision on random-agent trajectories yields a usable perceptual similarity function. Second, that same similarity function drives loop-closure shortcuts and adaptive waypoint selection. The shortcuts matter most: removing visual shortcuts drops validation success from 100/98/100 to 85/55/50 (Table 2). In Val-3 they cut the average shortest-path length to the goal from 990 to 155 steps. Temporally consistent (local-first) localization matters in larger mazes: per-frame localization gives 95/87/52 vs 100/98/100, attributed to perceptual aliasing. The learned retrieval network is essential; per-pixel matching (SeqSLAM-style) creates catastrophically wrong shortcuts and gets 1-10% success. The learned locomotion network plus shortcuts beats teach-and-repeat with recorded actions (45/36/30). Hyperparameter sweeps show the shortcut-matching smoothing window and memory subsampling are the sensitive knobs. Smoothing window 1 gives 100/70/26, and no subsampling gives 76/47/73.
method: Retrieval network R: siamese network with a ResNet-18 encoder per observation (512-d embeddings), concatenated and fed to a 4-hidden-layer MLP (512 units, ReLU) with a 2-way softmax. It is trained with cross-entropy to classify whether two observations are temporally close (≤ l=20 steps apart) or far (≥ M·l = 100 steps). Training data are random-agent trajectories, with no labels or rewards.

Memory graph G (non-parametric): one node per (4x-subsampled) observation of the ~5-min walkthrough. Edges link consecutive steps plus visual shortcuts where R similarity exceeds s_shortcut. The threshold is set so that the top 2000 pairs are connected. Shortcuts require |i−j| > ΔT_l = 5, and robustness comes from the median R score over a matched sequence window ΔT_w = 10 (loop closure).

Localization: the goal is localized once per episode. The agent is localized by the median of the k=5 nearest neighbours using precomputed embeddings, searching first in a local neighbourhood of the previous localization. It falls back to global search if the best similarity is below s_local = 0.7, which gives temporal consistency against perceptual aliasing.

Planning and waypoint selection: Dijkstra shortest path from the agent node to the goal node, with shortest paths precomputed once per episode. The waypoint is the furthest path vertex i ∈ [H_min=1, H_max=7] with R(o, o_i) > s_reach = 0.95, which avoids waypoints that are too close or unreachable.

Locomotion network L: a ResNet-18 over the channel-concatenated current and waypoint observations, followed by an FC layer with a 7-way softmax. It is trained self-supervised on random-agent pairs ((o_i, o_j), a_i) with |i−j| ≤ 20, learning P(a | o_t, o_t+k). Actions are sampled stochastically.

Training details: observations are stacks of 2 consecutive 160×120 RGB frames. Data are generated online by a random agent (action repeat 4) into a replay buffer of size 10,000. Optimization uses Adam (lr 1e-4) with batch 64, for 1M iterations (R) and 2M iterations (L).

setting.backbone: Two ResNet-18-based networks trained from scratch, self-supervised: a siamese retrieval network R with an MLP head, and a locomotion network L.
setting.model_size: two ResNet-18-based networks (parameter count not stated)
setting.training_data: Random-agent trajectories generated online in a single ViZDoom training maze layout, with 400 versions of randomized goal placements and textures. No labels or rewards are used. R is trained for 1M and L for 2M mini-batch iterations of 64 pairs. At test time the agent receives a ~5-min human walkthrough (10,500 simulation steps, images only) of each new maze to build the graph.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB (stack of 2 consecutive 160×120 frames) + goal image; no depth, pose or ego-motion
setting.action_space: 7 discrete actions (do nothing, move forward/backward/left/right, turn left/right) with action repeat 4
setting.privileged: Pre-exploration: an image-only human walkthrough video (~5 min, 10,500 steps) of the test maze is given before navigation (same footage given to baselines). No GT pose, depth, map or ego-motion.

numbers.extra: Human walkthrough (~5 min, 10,500 steps) of each test maze given beforehand. 7 unseen test mazes × 96 trials (4 starts × 4 goals × 6 repeats). Success = reach goal within 5,000 simulation steps.

numbers_note: This is a custom ViZDoom maze benchmark, not a standard embodied-nav benchmark, and the only metric is success rate within 5,000 steps. Success-vs-trial-duration curves appear only in figures (Fig. 5 for test, Fig. S2 for val). The homogeneous-texture variant also reports Val-3 = 55 (Table S2). Table S1 gives a hyperparameter sweep on val. Table S3 gives extra val ablations: per-pixel comparison with normalization 6/2/1, without normalization 10/8/7, and teach-and-repeat 45/36/30.
results: SPTM reaches 100% success on all 7 unseen test mazes, a mean of 100 vs 33.9 for the best baseline (goal-agnostic A3C LSTM). This is roughly three times better. It also beats goal-seeking feedforward (24.9, Zhu et al.-style) and goal-seeking LSTM (22, Mirowski et al.-style), which cannot exploit the 10k-step walkthrough. Performance holds up reasonably with autonomously generated walkthroughs (91-94% on 3 test mazes) and degrades more with homogeneous textures (75-98%).
limitations: Requires a pre-recorded exploration walkthrough of each test environment (human-generated in the main results). Autonomous exploration is only tested with RL baselines on simple mazes.

Memory grows linearly with exploration duration, and vision-only localization suffers from perceptual aliasing in large or low-texture environments. Performance drops with homogeneous textures, and some trajectories contain unnecessary loops.
Evaluated only in synthetic ViZDoom mazes with a single training layout, 7 test mazes and success rate as the only metric. The system is not end-to-end trainable and uses no ego-motion.
